articles.title: GTA 6 Shows 'What the American Dream Looks Like Now' in a Game Without Background Characters
articles.excerpt: New interview reveals Grand Theft Auto 6 put hundreds of hours into NPC design and dialogue and tried its best to make an accurate-to-the-times GTA.
articles.body: From what we've seen so far about Grand Theft Auto 6 , it looks like one of the biggest open-world games in history. When developers have to create such sprawling virtual environments, there's a risk of them feeling empty or repetitive, but that doesn't seem to be the case with GTA 6 . In a recent interview with Love Magazine, whose bits and screenshots have been shared by fans online , Rockstar revealed interesting details about the effort behind creating such a realistic world, with many stories and highly detailed characters. It also shared more about Lucia and Jason's hopes and dreams of fulfilling their American dream.

articles.excerpt: Nakodo reads websites it does not own. Three different places in the app do it: the brand's own site, pasted into onboarding, to write the search brief a creator's linked site, looking for the busines…
articles.body: Nakodo reads websites it does not own. Three different places in the app do it: the brand's own site, pasted into onboarding, to write the search brief a creator's linked site, looking for the business email they published public TikTok profile pages Every one of those URLs comes from outside. A brand types its domain. A creator puts a link in a bio. That makes all of them the same class of input as a form field, and it makes the plain global fetch() the wrong tool, for a reason that is not obvious until you go looking for it. The hole in check-then-fetch The naive version of SSRF protection is: resolve the hostname, check the address is public, then fetch. const { address } = await dns . promises .

articles.title: How much of your ML workflow is still held together manually?
articles.excerpt: I've been working on a DataOps/MLOps product called Datryc, and before we go much further with it, I want to challenge some of the assumptions we're making. The idea came from a fairly simple observat…
articles.body: I've been working on a DataOps/MLOps product called Datryc, and before we go much further with it, I want to challenge some of the assumptions we're making. The idea came from a fairly simple observation: getting from raw data to a model running somewhere involves much more than just training the model. You may need to: connect to different data sources; validate and clean the data; build preprocessing pipelines; monitor data quality; train and evaluate models; version model artifacts; deploy models for inference; monitor what happens afterward. There are excellent tools solving individual parts of this problem. What I'm interested in is the integration cost between those parts.
articles.author: Armen-Aris Shahinyan

articles.title: AgentCore Runtime Instances: GPU Colocation and Persistent State for Multi-Agent Workflows
articles.excerpt: AWS just published a detailed walkthrough of AgentCore Runtime Instances, showing how they deploy multi-agent workflows on persistent GPU infrastructure. The example is a three-agent music production…
articles.body: AWS just published a detailed walkthrough of AgentCore Runtime Instances, showing how they deploy multi-agent workflows on persistent GPU infrastructure. The example is a three-agent music production pipeline where agents colocate on one EC2 instance, share a filesystem, and hand work to each other over multiple days. This is not about payment authorization or spending limits (covered in previous AgentCore coverage). This is about the runtime plumbing: how agents share a GPU, how state persists across sessions, and how the orchestration layer decides when to hand work between agents versus spawning parallel execution.

articles.title: Pi Pod's Sandbox Architecture: Self-Hosted Agent Execution with Network and Secret Isolation
articles.excerpt: Pi Pod wraps the Pi coding agent framework in isolated sandboxes that run on your own server. Pi is a minimal, customizable agent harness (its configuration and tool integration layer) designed for de…
articles.body: Pi Pod wraps the Pi coding agent framework in isolated sandboxes that run on your own server. Pi is a minimal, customizable agent harness (its configuration and tool integration layer) designed for developers who want control over their agent runtime. Pi Pod addresses a specific gap: Pi's harness is minimal by design, but production agent deployments need sandboxing, secret management, network boundaries, and observability. Pi Pod provides those layers without forcing you into a cloud vendor's execution model. The architecture matters because self-hosted sandboxing gives you control over the blast radius when an agent misbehaves, leaks credentials, or attempts network exfiltration.

articles.title: Treat image prompts like functions: what 1,446 shared prompts say about templates
articles.excerpt: Most people write an AI image prompt the way they'd write a search query: once, for one result, then throw it away. The prompts that get shared and reused look different. We went through 1,446 popular…
articles.body: Most people write an AI image prompt the way they'd write a search query: once, for one result, then throw it away. The prompts that get shared and reused look different. We went through 1,446 popular image prompts in an openly licensed dataset, and a lot of them are written more like code than like sentences. Two patterns that stood out About 22% are templates. 323 of the 1,446 prompts contain at least one placeholder in square brackets, such as [OBJECT] , [COLOR] , [COUNTRY] or [BRAND NAME] . The author wrote the structure once and left slots for the parts that change. About 21% are written as JSON. 299 prompts are structured objects with keys for things like the scene, lighting and camera, rather than a paragraph. They're also long. The median prompt is about 1,000 characters.
articles.author: Ethan Brooks

articles.title: Our outreach address stopped being unguessable, so a reply now has to prove it belongs to the thread
articles.excerpt: Nakodo emails creators on a brand's behalf and each conversation has its own address on our sending domain. I wrote about why each thread gets its own address a couple of days ago: Reply-To is a sugge…
articles.body: Nakodo emails creators on a brand's behalf and each conversation has its own address on our sending domain. I wrote about why each thread gets its own address a couple of days ago: Reply-To is a suggestion that mail clients are free to ignore, so the From has to be the thing that identifies the conversation. The address in that post was acme-coffee-q7mkz3xpt2vn@nakodo.app . Twelve characters from a 31 character alphabet, about 59 bits, impossible to guess. It is also obviously a robot. A creator who looks at the sender before replying sees a machine, and the first thing we ask them to do is treat the email as a real approach from a real brand. So the address a thread writes from is now this instead: acme-coffee-outreach-12@nakodo.app That reads like a mailbox at a company.

articles.title: Every app on your Mac is talking to the internet - I built a map of it (zero telemetry)
articles.excerpt: Your Mac makes hundreds of outbound connections every hour — updaters, analytics SDKs, crash reporters, CDNs. None of it is visible unless you go looking. lsof -i gives you a wall of IPs. Little Snitc…
articles.body: Your Mac makes hundreds of outbound connections every hour — updaters, analytics SDKs, crash reporters, CDNs. None of it is visible unless you go looking. lsof -i gives you a wall of IPs. Little Snitch gives you prompts, a firewall, and a €59 price tag. We wanted something in between: see everything, block nothing, send nothing . So we built Snitch — an open-source, local-first network traffic visualizer for macOS.

articles.title: 31 Years Later, One of the Most Disturbing Thrillers Ever Made Is Officially Free on Streaming
articles.excerpt: Forget the Eli Roth movie, this 1995 horror movie belongs in the pantheon of so-bad-it's-good classics.
articles.body: Released in 1995, Ice Cream Man is the type of so-bad-it's-good horror movie that rarely gets made in the post- Get Out era where the genre is taken much more seriously. Directed by pornographer Paul Norman, who hoped this was his pivot to kid-friendly horror flicks, Ice Cream Man is a movie where a deranged killer mixes up bugs, human remains, and ice cream and feeds it to children. It's also a movie that spends a remarkable amount of time showing us what shoes everyone is wearing, as per a sponsorship agreement with Converse that probably cost some poor sneaker executive his job. Norman may have wanted to escape X-rated film, but he wound up making one of the creepiest stories ever put on film.

articles.body: Every mystery box has the same inherent problem: Eventually, you have to open it. The questions that keep an audience obsessing over a TV show from week to week can lose their power the moment we finally get some answers. Explain too little, and viewers feel frustrated. Explain too much, and you run the risk of deflating the entire story. There’s always the third option, however, which is to answer questions with details that generate even more questions. Instead of a mystery box, why not make it a nesting doll of secrets?

articles.title: People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough?
articles.excerpt: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he…
articles.body: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.” “I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype , steered by zealots , inescapable . The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now. On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast.

articles.body: StarSkirmish pits AI-made StarCraft-playing bots against one another, as well as against human-made bots. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were essentially tied as the best-performing AI-made bots, but they couldn't top Stardust, the top-rated human-made bot. On Friday, GPT was facing off against Claude and the human-created bot Pluto, but according to Kotaku , it couldn't quite get an edge. So it resorted to a tactic that is becoming alarmingly common for modern AI models - it broke the rules . GPT-6 Astra went and downloaded Stardust, and started running that instead of its own bot.
